subject: Statistical tests for closest relative estimation of unknown specimen?

messages.author: 57bc58593a19897f
messages.subject: Statistical tests for closest relative estimation of unknown specimen?
parts:
Dear geomorph community, 

I hope you can help me yet again! 

I have 499 sliding semilandmarks from in total 107 scapulae to capture the whole shape. The dataset includes human, gorilla, chimp, and orangutan. From the consensus shape, I have estimated the shape of the branch ancestor, and then warped the landmarks to a surface, showing what the scapula estimation would have looked like if it existed. Using this ancestral shape reconstruction (ASR) as a reference, I have mapped currently living species 'onto' it, which shows how current shapes vary from the ancestral shapes: 

However, this is only a visualization. 

I am seeking a function that can statistically test what group the ASR would fall into if it was in the dataset - like which species it is morphologically closest to based on my landmarks. I am considering plotting it into a PCA morphospace using convex hulls, but I am dreaming about a function where I ask "what group is this shape closest to?" and it would spit out an answer. 

Crossing my fingers that I am not too fluffy about this and that you have creative ideas for my next step! 

Sincerely, 
Stine

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Statistical tests for closest relative estimation of unknown specimen?
parts:
Dear Stine,

The simplest answer to your question is, yes, of course, a linear discrimination analysis can be performed on a set of training data, and you can obtain posterior classification probabilities for the test subject, for its classification in each group.  This is fairly straightforward, so long as the test specimen is not used to define the the discriminant functions; i.e., do not suppose it belongs to group X to build the model with the training data and then be surprised that the posterior classification probability for group X is high.  The MASS::lda function is good about allowing cross-validation (where each specimen is left out of training data and then tested using the functions obtained from the other specimens).  The RRPP::prep.lda function will allow one to use a procD.lm object to use the MASS::lda function.

The complicated parts arise with HOW to go about this with GM data.  There are basically two methods.  One is to allow the one specimen to be part of the sample on which GPA is performed, so that it is best aligned to the consensus (mean).  However, this approach allows the specimen to contribute to the calculation of the mean, and therefore, is not in the spirit of avoiding circular reasoning, as one attempts to do with cross-validation in the linear discriminant analysis.  The other is to perform GPA on all specimens except the test specimen, then align the test specimen configuration divided by its centroid size to the consensus configuration from the GPA.  This removes the potential circularity of performing a GPA that includes the test subject, but then the alignment of the single specimen is maybe not as optimal as it would be if it were included in the GPA, so one would have to consider a higher probability of mis-assignment to a correct group as a potential type II error.  The increased probability of a type II error would be of little concern if many specimens were used for the GPA; i.e., the mean would not change much whether using n - 1 or n specimens.

I have no recommendation for one method over the other, and if both presented similar results, it would not matter much.  Regardless, yes, linear discriminant analysis could be used for your purpose.  Keep in mind you would probably have to use a set of PC scores with high-dimensional data to avoid singular covariance matrices, which are inverted as part of the classification.  The RRPP::prep.lda function can help with that.

Good luck!
Mike

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Statistical tests for closest relative estimation of unknown specimen?
parts:
Dear Stine,

First , in order to cite R packages, I recommend doing this:

citation(“MASS”)
citation(“RRPP”)

Second, for citing methods, this is an interesting thing to consider.  You could consider citing work that has used a canonical variates analysis (CVA) for morphometric data, but I would discourage this without verifying that the work you cite calculates posterior classification probabilities.  Many software packages do not, but instead use simply classification based on minimal Malanahobis distance to group means.  This implicitly assumes that prior probabilities are equal, and wrests control of such important considerations from the researchers.  Furthermore, CVA software/functions might promote ordination more so than classification, which can lead to improper uses, like calling the canonical space a “morphopsace”.  There are two morphometric R packages that allow flexibility for shape data classification — RRPP and Morpho — and I’ll explain their differences below.

I would cite the following:

Mitteroecker, P., & Bookstein, F. (2011). Linear discrimination, ordination, and the visualization of selection gradients in modern morphometrics. Evolutionary Biology, 38, 100-114.

This paper does discuss classification in some detail.  But I would also search using the terms “linear discriminant multivariate classification” to find a textbook that properly discusses using prior probabilities in a Bayesian framework. 

As for the differences between RRPP and Morpho, in most cases, there are none or few.  Morpho does a good job of recapitulating the results that MASS::lda function would provide, via the Morpho::CVA function, also using the Morpho::classify function.  Rather than reinvent wheels, we decided the MASS::lda function was sufficient, but the RRPP::prep.lda function allows one to have a linear model that estimates LS means rather than just simple means, unlike any other package.  For example, one could have a linear model that is shape ~ size + group and perform LDA without having to ignore size.  One could use a backdoor approach to do this with other functions, but would have to obtain size-adjusted shape values first to use MASS::lda or Morpho::CVA in this way.  The prep.lda function does that, inherently.

hope that helps!
Mike
